name: Septorhinoplasty

card.summary: Combined surgery on the nasal septum and the outer nose, done for breathing and shape together; the evidence base is mostly surgical case series, with recovery details well documented.
card.note: Surgical procedure under anaesthesia; swelling and tip position can take months to a year to settle, and revision surgery is a documented possibility.

quick.overview:
Septorhinoplasty combines septoplasty (straightening the cartilage and bone wall inside the nose) with rhinoplasty (reshaping the outside of the nose). It is performed when a person has both a breathing problem from a deviated septum and a wish to change nasal appearance, such as a crooked bridge after a past injury.

On looksmaxxing forums it appears in threads where members ask whether they need a plain rhinoplasty or the combined operation, and in recovery threads about swelling and tip position. Published research on it is largely surgical series and trials of peri-operative care rather than comparisons of cosmetic outcomes.
quick.mechanism: The surgeon works on the septum to correct deviation and on the nasal cartilages and bones to alter the external shape, using an open or closed approach. Cartilage from the septum is often reused as graft material, and the nasal bones may be repositioned.
quick.risks: Documented issues include bruising and swelling, persisting obstruction (sometimes linked to enlarged turbinates), the need for revision surgery, and anaesthesia-related effects such as sore throat. It is a prescription-level surgical procedure performed by licensed surgeons; outcomes vary by surgeon and anatomy.

lead: Septorhinoplasty is an operation that combines septoplasty, which corrects a deviated nasal septum, with rhinoplasty, which reshapes the external nose. It is used when a patient has both an obstructed airway and an aesthetic concern, for example a crooked nose following trauma.[1][2] Surgeons describe it as a common functional-aesthetic procedure, and trials registered in several countries study its recovery, pain control and outcomes.[3][4]

The published evidence mostly consists of surgical technique reports, retrospective reviews and randomised trials of adjuncts such as tranexamic acid, corticosteroids, analgesia and anaesthetic methods, rather than head-to-head tests of aesthetic results.[5][6][7] A review of septal surgery noted that, although its benefit seems intuitive, relatively few papers had confirmed it when the review was written.[8]
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed mainly by people deciding between a rhinoplasty alone and the combined operation, and by people describing post-operative swelling and tip rotation.[9][10]

paras: The septum is the cartilage-and-bone partition that divides the nasal cavity. When it is deviated, the airway on one side can be narrowed. Septoplasty straightens or removes the deviated portions; rhinoplasty alters the shape of the nasal bones, cartilages and tip. In septorhinoplasty both are done in one session.[1][11]

Surgeons may use the external (open) or endonasal (closed) approach. A general rhinoplasty reference notes that systematic reviews have not found significant long-term differences in functional or aesthetic scores between open and closed approaches.[12]

Technique reports describe methods for lower-third nasal work, such as the tongue-in-groove technique, which a 10-year experience paper presents as a way to correct excess columellar show and maintain correction of caudal deviation while controlling tip rotation and projection.[13] Septal cartilage composition has also been studied because the septum is a common graft source.[14] Reports exist of repairing septal perforations through the external septorhinoplasty approach.[15]

A review of inferior turbinate hypertrophy notes that nasal obstruction can persist after a technically sound septorhinoplasty if enlarged turbinates are not addressed, and that management of turbinate hypertrophy has been debated for over a century.[16] Registered trials have compared septorhinoplasty with and without turbinate surgery for such patients.[17][18]

A randomised study in septorhinoplasty patients examined tranexamic acid and corticosteroid for post-operative swelling and bruising.[7] Other trials in patients undergoing septorhinoplasty have tested a ketamine gargle for post-operative sore throat after intubation and nitrous oxide for opioid-induced hyperalgesia after remifentanil-propofol anaesthesia.[5][6] A review addressed the evidence for peri-operative antibiotics in otolaryngology.[19] Registered trials are examining nerve blocks, liposomal bupivacaine, fibrin glue and pain-score courses after the operation.[20][21][22][23]
Swelling after rhinoplasty can take a year or more to fully resolve, according to a general rhinoplasty reference.[12]

A study of cosmetic rhinoplasty at a plastic surgery group practice examined revision rates and risk factors for dissatisfaction and complications.[24] A general reference puts failure of primary rhinoplasty requiring further surgery at 5 to 20 percent of operations.[12]

Human studies of septorhinoplasty include: a retrospective multi-hospital review of septal surgery efficacy (which excluded septorhinoplasty but frames the evidence for septal work)[8]; a 10-year series on the tongue-in-groove technique[13]; randomised trials of tranexamic acid and corticosteroid on swelling and bruising[7], ketamine gargle for sore throat[5] and nitrous oxide for hyperalgesia[6]; and registered trials covering allergic rhinitis outcomes, turbinate surgery quality of life, pain management and a 750-patient outcome analysis.[18][17][20][21][25]
Most trials focus on peri-operative issues or functional measures. Long-term aesthetic comparison data are limited in the sources reviewed.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the topic appears as planning questions (which operation to book, how it interacts with orthodontics) and post-operative recovery reports.[9][10]

claims.claim: A crooked nose with a slightly deviated septum calls for septorhinoplasty rather than rhinoplasty alone.
claims.believers: A poster in a planning thread reasons that a plain rhinoplasty would leave the deviated septum, which could affect the nose again, and asks whether the combined operation is the better choice.[9]
claims.experts: Surgical literature describes septorhinoplasty as the combined operation for septal deviation with external deformity.[1][2] Individual recommendations depend on examination, and no source reviewed provides a general rule.

claims.claim: Braces or aligners should be timed relative to nose surgery because they could put pressure on the nose.
claims.believers: The same poster says they have read that braces can put pressure on the nose and asks whether orthodontics should come first.[9]
claims.experts: No study in the reviewed sources examines the sequencing of orthodontic treatment and septorhinoplasty.

claims.claim: A very upturned tip right after surgery is normal and drops over time.
claims.believers: Members who have had the surgery say the tip drops back, with reported times ranging from about a week to six months or more.[10]
claims.experts: A general rhinoplasty reference states that swelling can take at least a year to resolve.[12] No study in the reviewed sources quantifies tip rotation change.

claims.claim: Telling the surgeon repeatedly not to make the nose upturned gives a natural, straight result.
claims.believers: One member reports being happy with a natural-looking, straight outcome after repeating this instruction and choosing a good surgeon.[9]
claims.experts: Surgical series describe techniques for controlling tip rotation and projection.[13] Patient satisfaction after nasal surgery varies; revision rates are documented.[24]
